findings.title: Findings converge on `_consider` as the one filter for listed candidates
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger's central sentence says every candidate from either source still goes through `_FileSelector._consider`, which keeps symlink handling, containment, and excludes. `_consider` was written for paths the walker had already pruned and for paths a person named. A flat git list is neither, and it fails in three separate ways: its directory branch recurses into submodules and nested clones, its symlink check runs before its exclude check, and its exclude check runs after every stat call. Each finding proposes its own patch to the function. Should the design re-evaluate how listed candidates are filtered, rather than patch `_consider` three times?
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate how listed candidates are filtered before addressing Findings 2, 3, and 4 individually. Open questions: which checks a listed candidate needs and in what order; what `_consider` is still for; whether `explicit_paths` still describes the origins; which spelling of the path excludes match against.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate how listed candidates are filtered before addressing Findings 2, 3, and 4 individually

findings.title: Gitlink and nested-clone entries re-enter `_walk`, so D7's "not scanned" doesn't hold as written
findings.why_it_matters: D7 (are submodules and nested clones scanned?) was ratified as "drop directory entries silently", but the Summary sends every candidate through `_consider`, whose directory branch calls `_walk`. `_walk` is where the listing is called from, and a submodule or nested clone has its own `.git`. Probe: a full listing prints `vendor` and `nested/`, and a listing with its working directory in `vendor` prints the submodule's files. Built as written, third-party code lands in findings, which is the outcome D7 chose to avoid.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A directory symlink inside an excluded tree becomes exit 3, because `_consider` checks symlinks before excludes
findings.why_it_matters: Today the walker drops an excluded directory before it looks at symlinks, and says so in its docstring. In `_consider` the order is reversed: `is_symlink and is_dir` records "directory symlink is not traversed" at line 580, before any exclude check. Git lists a directory symlink as a plain path (probe: `linkdir` and `vendored/link`), so one inside `.venv/` or a configured `exclude` that git still lists turns a clean run into exit 3 in hooks, CI, and JSON consumers. The contract critic's first proposed fix, moving `_is_path_ignored` earlier, doesn't work for its own `vendor/link -> ../x` example: `_is_path_ignored` receives the resolved path (discovery.py:562, :604), which is outside `vendor/`, so it isn't excluded.
findings.recommended: A: Match excludes against the listed path and its ancestors before any filesystem call, and say so in the ledger.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Excluded trees git still lists are stat'ed file by file, against a documented promise
findings.why_it_matters: `docs/configuration.md:83` says an ignored directory "is skipped without being enumerated, which is what keeps a large `.venv/` or `node_modules/` cheap". Inside a repo that stops being true for an unignored one: `ls-files --others` lists each file, and `_consider` runs `exists`, `resolve`, and three stat calls before the exclude check. Measured on 50,000 unignored files: `ls-files` took 0.09 s, and the stat calls took 2.4 s. So the cost is `_consider`'s order, not git, and the critic's "multi-minute" is overstated. Separately, the plain walk has to keep directory-level pruning: D3 deletes `_ignored`, which `_traversable_dirs` calls, and D3's "match the path and each ancestor" applied per file would enumerate `node_modules` in full outside a repo.
findings.recommended: A: Check excludes on the listed path first, keep directory pruning in the plain walk, and rewrite the docs promise for the listing case.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A directory that git ignores scans zero files with exit 0, while a file inside it gets linted
findings.why_it_matters: D2's deciding factor is "a person who names a file gets it linted". For directories the ledger routes through git instead. Probe, with an untracked `build/gen.py` under an ignored `build/`: listing from inside `build/` prints nothing and exits 0. So `check build/gen.py` lints the file, `check build/*.py` lints it, and `check build/` reports zero files with exit 0, because `fail_on_empty` is off by default. The empty-scan guidance is also suppressed when explicit paths are given, so nothing points at the cause. `include = ["build"]` and a `--root` inside an ignored folder behave the same way, including any project without its own `.git` under a dotfiles repo whose `.gitignore` is `*`. D2's Situation does say named directories are listed through git, but the ratified sentence accepts the file case only, and it never names this outcome.
findings.recommended: A: A directory git reports as ignored gets the plain walk when it is named, in `include`, or the root.
findings.chosen: A: A directory git reports as ignored gets the plain walk when it is named, in include, or the root

findings.title: Git's warnings on a successful listing vanish, and unreadable directories drop out silently
findings.why_it_matters: Posture says loud failure, but the ledger defines failure as a non-zero exit. Probe with a `chmod 000` directory: `ls-files` prints `warning: could not open directory 'locked/': Permission denied`, exits 0, and omits the file. Today `os.walk`'s `onerror` records that as a traversal error, which is exit 3. After this change the same tree exits 0 with files missing and no signal.
findings.recommended: A: Turn non-empty stderr on exit 0 into a recorded discovery error, carrying git's text.
findings.chosen: A: Turn non-empty stderr on exit 0 into a recorded discovery error, carrying git's text

findings.title: A missing git binary becomes an opaque internal error rather than D1's promised message
findings.why_it_matters: D1's table promises that with git not installed inside a repo the run "stops, and says `--no-gitignore` walks instead". But `subprocess` raises `FileNotFoundError` (probe) rather than returning an exit code. `run_scan` catches only `DiscoveryError`, so it reaches the CLI's process boundary and becomes an internal error, exit 4, with a traceback only under `--debug`.
findings.chosen: In D1's Recommendation, after "The error carries git's stderr and names `--no-gitignore`", add: "A failure to start git (`OSError`, including a missing binary) is the same discovery error, with the same hint."

findings.title: The `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer list omits most of the ratified breaks and the one-footer format
findings.why_it_matters: The Summary names three behaviours the footer has to cover, which are the ones that follow from replacing the matcher. D1, D2, D3, D5, D7, and D8 each ratify another break: git as a runtime dependency with `.git` failures at exit 3, named ignored files linted, `!` in `exclude` as a config error, `files_skipped` removed, submodules unscanned, and `--no-gitignore` dropping `.git/info/exclude` and global excludes. release-please surfaces only the first footer, and only the PR body reaches it, so a builder following the list ships a changelog missing most of this. `README.md:113` also promises "without shelling out to git", which the "Also updated" list doesn't name specifically.
findings.chosen: After the three bullets at design.md:17-19, add one line: "The footer also names the breaks D1, D2, D3, D5, D7, and D8 accept, as one `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer with a `####` list per `.claude/rules/changelog-quality.md`." In the `README.md` bullet at design.md:27, add "and the 'without shelling out to git' sentence".

findings.title: D5's `schema_version` bump doesn't say which of the two JSON outputs moves
findings.why_it_matters: `check` JSON and `rules` JSON each emit their own `schema_version: 1`. D5 removes `files_skipped` from `check` output only, and says "bump `schema_version` to 2" with no scope. Tests pin both, and `docs/configuration.md:76`, `:113` and `reporters/json.py:21` define extra keys as outside "the `schema_version: 1` contract", so they need rewording either way. (The critic's further point that #60's pickup must remember a new number doesn't apply: spec 005 line 476 says only "a `schema_version` bump" and names no number.)
findings.recommended: A: Bump only the `check` output; `rules` stays at 1. Reword the `schema_version: 1` references to match.
findings.chosen: A: Bump only the check output; rules stays at 1

findings.title: D3's "correct rather than approximately correct" is false for at least one pattern shape, and the ancestor probe is unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: D3's Recommendation says that removing negation makes the simple matcher "correct rather than approximately correct". Probe, using `GitIgnoreSpec` with an ancestor walk against `git check-ignore`: eight of eleven no-negation cases agree. `build/**` diverges only on the directory itself, which is harmless, since its contents are excluded either way. An escaped trailing space diverges for real in the other two cases: a pattern ending in two backslashes and a space matches different paths than git's, in both directions, because D3 deletes `_trailing_whitespace_trimmed`, which corrected exactly this. Directory-only patterns also need the ancestor probe to carry a trailing `/` (as `_match_patterns` does today), and D3 doesn't say so.
findings.chosen: In D3's Recommendation, replace "so the simple matcher is correct rather than approximately correct" with "so the simple matcher agrees with git for the shapes in D4's parity table; a pattern with an escaped trailing space is a known divergence, recorded in the docs' divergence table". In D3's option A cell, add that ancestors are probed in directory form (trailing `/`).

findings.title: Which discovery mode ran is invisible, though the ledger's own motivating case is CI differing from a laptop
findings.why_it_matters: Whether `.gitignore` is honoured now depends on a filesystem probe, and D5 removes `files_skipped`, the one number that hinted at it. A reader of a CI log can't tell whether a run listed through git or walked. Posture says no new logging, because a person watches this CLI.
findings.chosen: Side A: No mode reporting

findings.title: Listing a tree runs a command from that tree's `.git/config` through `core.fsmonitor`
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: users who lint trees they did not create (downloaded archives, CI checkouts of untrusted forks). Until now house-lint only read files. Probe: with `core.fsmonitor` set to a script in the repo's `.git/config`, `git ls-files` ran the script; with `-c core.fsmonitor=false`, it didn't. The critic couldn't confirm this, and it is confirmed. git's ownership check doesn't help, since a tree the current user extracted passes it. D1's table already cites this config as the reason to reject option C, and it applies equally to a same-owner tree under the chosen option A.
findings.recommended: A: Pass `-c core.fsmonitor=false` on the listing call.
findings.chosen: A: Pass -c core.fsmonitor=false on the listing call

findings.title: D1's marker walk guesses at git's repo discovery, and misses both ways in rare setups
findings.why_it_matters: D1 infers "git will treat this as a repo" from a `.git` entry. With `GIT_DIR` exported and no `.git` entry on the path, git would list (probe: it listed the other repo's index), but the marker walk finds nothing, so discovery does a plain walk and scans gitignored files with no error. That is the quiet divergence D1's deciding factor rules out. D1's sentence that an empty `.git` directory "also stops the run" is also only partly true: probe, with an empty `.git` directory below a real repo, git skips it and lists through the outer repo, exit 0. It stops only when no repo sits above. The dangling `.git` file and stray-ancestor cases are D1's accepted stance (probe: dangling exits 128), and an unrelated ancestor's ignore rules are design.md:19's accepted change; the zero-file form of that is in Finding 5.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an exported `GIT_DIR` with no `.git` entry gets the plain walk, and an empty `.git` directory below a real repo lists through that repo.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: `include` entries that are files lose their gitignore check, which the ledger doesn't list
findings.why_it_matters: D2 covers files named on the CLI. `include = ["gen.py"]` reaches `_consider` the same way with `explicit_paths=False`. Today a gitignored one is skipped at line 623. Once the matcher is gone, listing only applies to directories, so it gets linted. That is a further behaviour change the ledger doesn't state.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a gitignored file named in `include` is linted.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The empty-scan guidance points at `include` when the cause is a submodule
findings.why_it_matters: `zero_file_guidance` points only at `include` and the config file. Under D7 a scan can come up empty because all the Python lives in a submodule or nested clone, and under `--fail-on-empty` the user gets exit 1 with advice about `include`. The exit-code logic doesn't change; only the message misdirects.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an empty scan caused by submodules still points at `include`.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The test rewrite is larger than the ledger's Build list suggests
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a reviewer who must scope the PR. `tests/unit/test_discovery.py` has 72 lines mentioning `.gitignore` and no `git init`, so those tests have to move to a real repo fixture under the "not a repo" rule. `files_skipped` asserts appear on 23 lines across `test_discovery.py`, `test_cli.py`, and `test_scan_pipeline.py`. D4 counts only the parity and fuzz files, and `test_pre_commit_hook.py` has no gitignore coverage for D2's hook claim. These tests fail loudly when the code changes, so the critic's "silently stop honoring" overstates it: the builder finds them on the first run.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the ledger doesn't size the test rewrite; the build finds it from test failures.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation
